title: Civil justice: Capacity gains need human safeguards
desc: Frames AI as redirecting scarce professional time and providing bounded self-help, not replacing comprehensive representation.

kps.k: The central proposition is to expand meaningful legal help, not merely improve lawyers’ productivity.
kps.d: Nori, Malhan and Gupta, and Susskind’s reported summit address place underserved people’s problems, prevention and resolution at the centre of AI design. They argue that faster existing workflows alone will not overcome cost, eligibility, language and navigation barriers. Nicole Black nevertheless treats general workflow tools, tools tailored to underserved clients’ lawyers, and direct consumer information as complementary routes. The disagreement concerns whether efficiency within existing institutions is sufficient, rather than whether it has any value.

qs.q: But if you take a step back and look at the problem, helping lawyers work a little better isn’t going to solve the access to justice gap.
qs.a: Sateesh Nori Joins LawDroid: AI Tools for Access to Justice, Housing Court, and Legal Aid · Access to justice · 2026

qs.q: This forward-looking perspective urged the community to avoid merely automating the past and instead use technology to design a more accessible, preventative, and outcome-focused system of justice.
qs.a: AI+A2J 2025 Summit Takeaways · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Unmet need supports a capacity-expansion argument, but the cited statistics have different populations and evidentiary bases.
kps.d: In the Behnke discussion, Flagg attributes to LSC the finding that 92% of problems affecting low-income Americans receive no or inadequate assistance. This is not equivalent to other speakers’ broader claims about all Americans being unable to afford lawyers or all civil needs going unmet. Nori’s estimates of roughly 1,000 clients represented and more than 10,000 turned away provide practitioner testimony, not independent population measurements. These accounts motivate experimentation; they do not measure AI’s impact.

qs.q: LSC did a justice gap report a few years back and found that 92% of the problems affecting low income Americans receive no or inadequate assistance.
qs.a: ABA President Michelle Behnke on How We Talk About Justice — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Maybe we should ask the 92 percent of Americans who can’t afford a lawyer whether they’d like a free or low-cost solution.
qs.a: Sateesh Nori & Tom Martin — legal aid, Depositron, and 'access to justice, not access to lawyers' · Access to justice · 2025

kps.k: AI-assisted legal aid could redirect scarce professional time toward advocacy, with some reported gains but limited evaluation detail.
kps.d: Nori and Colpoys propose automating intake, triage, drafting and administrative work to increase capacity and reduce burnout while preserving judgment, counselling and advocacy. Nori particularly favours more appellate work, conditional on fair initial hearings. The 2025 AI for Justice episode summary reports up to 15 attorney hours saved weekly, as many as 50% more clients served daily and urgent materials prepared up to 75% faster, alongside faster client relief. These are reported maxima from a provider-and-practitioner account without measurement methodology, not average or independently established effects. Most other capacity and wellbeing claims remain expectations.

qs.q: AI can handle the repetitive and standardized tasks that now consume attorneys’ time, freeing us to focus on the parts of practice that require judgment, empathy, and advocacy.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: We should be doing appeals, as long as people have viable ways to get claims heard fairly in the first place.
qs.a: Sateesh Nori Joins LawDroid: AI Tools for Access to Justice, Housing Court, and Legal Aid · Access to justice · 2026

kps.k: Public-facing tools offer bounded information and self-help, not demonstrated substitutes for comprehensive representation.
kps.d: Roxanne addresses New York City tenants’ repair-rights questions; Depositron supplies structured requests for withheld deposits; Martin describes Law Answers as constraining answers to a user-selected state. Slayton describes Court Help turning official court information into eviction-response instructions and form links. These examples establish reported capabilities, not measured recovery rates or litigation outcomes. Slayton and Leonard favour tiered assistance, with lawyers handling higher-stakes needs; Slayton cautions that information alone may suffice for only a small share of users. Young similarly identifies complexity and client vulnerability as limits on expansion.

qs.q: As we're sitting here speaking, you've just helped launch something called Roxanne, which is an AI-powered tool created with an organization called Housing Court Answers, and also using the technology company, Josef, to basically answer tenants' questions about repair rights under New York City law.
qs.a: Ep 275: Can AI Bridge the Justice Gap? Legal Aid Lawyer and Innovator Sateesh Nori Thinks So · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: So you can go on Court Help right now and say, “How do I file a response or an answer to an eviction case?” and it gives you step-by-step instructions and links to the forms.
qs.a: AI in LA Courts: David Slayton on Access to Justice — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The safety debate compares imperfect assistance with no help, while retaining questions about reliability and human intervention.
kps.d: McCormack reports the objection that consumer AI could institutionalise inferior justice; she, Moon and Nori counter that human services also fail and that people without help should inform the comparison. This does not establish AI’s comparative accuracy. McCormack separately worries about sycophantic responses, and contributors acknowledge hallucination and confidentiality risks. Flynn offers a practical oversight model: experts check and correct answers before launch, then monitor performance through workflows and triggers. Nori’s described triage deployment also remains human-mediated. Neither these safeguards nor jurisdiction selection demonstrate that hallucinations have been eliminated.

qs.q: The idea is that because these tools are imperfect or may make mistakes, they cement inequality.
qs.a: Sateesh Nori & Tom Martin — legal aid, Depositron, and 'access to justice, not access to lawyers' · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: Not perfect, perfect is the enemy of the good, but no help versus really good help.
qs.a: Talking AI for Access to Justice at the 25th Innovations in Technology Conference — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

kps.k: Affordable software does not resolve unequal implementation capacity or guarantee that commercial gains reach underserved users.
kps.d: Nori rejects an inevitable two-tier future, pointing to cheap or free tools and urging legal services to secure access. Contributors to the 2025 report warn that even open-source development requires funding, organisational capacity and leadership trust; unequal resources could widen gaps between nonprofits or between nonprofit and commercial providers. Black questions whether commercial incentives will deliver access benefits. Walker and the Alex Su conversation likewise express dissatisfaction with tool-focused innovation that has not sufficiently changed service delivery. Enterprise savings and internal legal-department triage remain distinct from evidence of reduced unmet civil legal need.

qs.q: But in terms of like dollar for dollar, these are extremely cheap if not free right now for us to test and to use.
qs.a: Ep 275: Can AI Bridge the Justice Gap? Legal Aid Lawyer and Innovator Sateesh Nori Thinks So · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: Developing AI tools, even with open-source models, requires capacity, funding, and trust from leadership.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Practical adoption centres on user research, shared infrastructure, training and sustained implementation work.
kps.d: Hagan describes interviews, hands-on user exercises and frontline-provider consultation to select uses and assess quality and risks before demonstration projects. Report contributors recommend shared knowledge bases, reusable blueprints and co-development; Malhan and Gupta favour responsible open-source entrepreneurship. Legal-aid discussions add procurement guidance, supported experimentation and realistic timelines: Oborn advises allowing an extra six months. These are implementation methods and recommendations, not proof of effectiveness. They imply that purchasing access alone cannot deliver the proposed benefits.

qs.q: So that's meant doing a lot of interviews, scenario exercises where we have people try out AI and rate it, talking to providers about what kinds of tasks and opportunities they think should be prioritized, if any, for generative AI R&D, and basically trying to identify an agenda of where AI might be useful or not and how to evaluate quality and risks for these prospective use cases.
qs.a: Margaret Hagan & Sateesh Nori — putting AI to the test for legal services: lab-to-pilot pipelines and the crisis case for urgency · Access to justice · 2024

qs.q: In addition, I feel strongly that larger organizations must be funding and co-developing this type of foundational infrastructure, making it easier for LSOs everywhere to integrate with shared tools, vetted knowledge bases, and pre-trained models.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Broader transformation raises unresolved choices about regulation, platform governance and sustainable delivery models.
kps.d: Nori calls for abolishing unauthorized-practice restrictions in his report contribution, while separately describing lawful, locally compliant independent services as a goal. His roughly $5 early-help app and Claimsy proposal—$10 per party for a rapid decision, potentially with a human adjudicator—remain business-model hypotheses, not achieved economics or outcomes. The summit account reports competing strategies toward major technology companies: close collaboration or stronger public-interest protections through regulation, taxation and licensing. Its call to redesign justice therefore extends beyond automation to who controls services, funds infrastructure and bears responsibility for public benefit; the supplied material does not settle those choices.

qs.q: And the need to abolish the outdated and exclusionary rules surrounding the unauthorized         practice of law.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: The other is building services like LawAnswers.ai that deliver legal help independently of lawyers and legal aid, accurate and efficient within the boundaries of the law where people live, and making it sustainable as a business model.
qs.a: Sateesh Nori Joins LawDroid: AI Tools for Access to Justice, Housing Court, and Legal Aid · Access to justice · 2026

vlens.an: The in-house counsel and legal-operations source constructively redirects the proposition from access to civil justice toward outcome-led transformation of enterprise legal-service delivery. Anderson shares several implementation instincts with the cluster: begin with the user’s problem rather than the technology, treat adoption as organisational change, and use a bounded frontline model combining self-help, interaction with an agent and AI-assisted triage. Those elements are analogous to the cluster’s tiered assistance and capacity-redirection model. The material difference is the objective and beneficiary: Microsoft Legal is serving internal commercial business clients and improving departmental operations, lawyer experience and request routing, not expanding meaningful legal help for underserved civil-justice users. The source also provides no evidence about access-to-justice outcomes, reliability safeguards, human verification or when comprehensive representation remains necessary. Because only one curated source is supplied for this professional voice, no cross-source consensus or internal variation can be inferred; within this source, the outcome-first and tiered-delivery elements align operationally with the proposition, while its enterprise focus redirects the proposition’s public-facing purpose.

qs.q: Don't start with AI, start with what the outcome is that you want to be.
qs.a: Inside Microsoft Legal: A Look at AI Use Built for Scale (Rebecca Anderson - Head of Legal EMEA Microsoft) · In-house counsel · 2026

qs.q: And so there, they can find self-help resources, they can interact with an agent, and there's also an entry point into a CRM system.
qs.a: Inside Microsoft Legal: A Look at AI Use Built for Scale (Rebecca Anderson - Head of Legal EMEA Microsoft) · In-house counsel · 2026

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources accept the proposition that AI should expand meaningful civil legal help rather than replace comprehensive representation. Their common rationale is that severe unmet need justifies experimentation, while responsible adoption requires understanding the technology’s limits and orienting it toward accessibility and better justice outcomes—not merely faster existing workflows. They materially develop the proposition in two ways: Perlman supplies an adoption pathway based on sustained, hands-on learning about capabilities and limitations; the summit account advances a broader redesign agenda covering prevention, outcomes and public-interest governance of Big Tech. There is internal variation in emphasis: the Perlman discussion is pragmatic and lawyer-centred, but offers neither deployment safeguards nor evidence of reduced unmet need; the summit source is more systemic, presenting both collaboration with technology companies and stronger regulation, taxation, licensing and public-interest protections, without resolving that strategic choice. Both are recommendations or forward-looking arguments rather than measured demonstrations of impact. This assessment concerns only the curated sources supplied and does not establish the prevalence of these views across academia and research.

qs.q: Use it for in your daily life so that you get a feel for what it can do, and just as importantly, what it can’t do.
qs.a: Do Existing Legal Ethics Rules Cover AI? — full episode transcript · Academia · 2024

qs.q: This forward-looking perspective urged the community to avoid merely automating the past and instead use technology to design a more accessible, preventative, and outcome-focused system of justice.

vlens.an: Across this curated set, the professional voice accepts the proposition that AI should expand meaningful civil legal help by redirecting scarce professional time and enabling bounded self-help, rather than merely making elite lawyers more productive. Its material contribution is operational: human-mediated triage copilots, user and frontline-provider research, targeted tools for high-volume tasks, procurement guidance, training, shared infrastructure and realistic implementation timelines. The common rationale is that intake, triage, drafting, translation and administration consume capacity that could instead support advocacy, counselling, trials, negotiation and complex questions. The sources also distinguish proposals and practitioner experience from demonstrated outcomes; even the reported legal-aid gains are upper-bound claims without detailed evaluation methodology. Internal variation concerns how bounded the model should remain. Several accounts expressly retain lawyers or other human operators for difficult or consequential work, while Nori and Martin sometimes envisage direct-to-public services operating independently of lawyers and, aspirationally, making gap-filling legal aid obsolete. That substitution-oriented strand sits uneasily with the cluster’s emphasis on comprehensive representation and human safeguards, but it does not displace the selected voice’s broader, concrete development of an augmentative and needs-led approach.

qs.q: So we built a co-pilot model for these operators so that the Gen AI can be in the background, like a really experienced supervisor, and can feed answers to the person who can then relay them to the caller as a first step.
qs.a: Margaret Hagan & Sateesh Nori — putting AI to the test for legal services: lab-to-pilot pipelines and the crisis case for urgency · Access to justice · 2024

qs.q: Sateesh Nori: This is controversial given my background, but I want to make legal aid obsolete.We exist as legal aid because there’s a gap.
qs.a: Sateesh Nori & Tom Martin — legal aid, Depositron, and 'access to justice, not access to lawyers' · Access to justice · 2025

vlens.an: These selected regulators, court leaders and professional-body voices accept the proposition that AI should expand meaningful legal help by augmenting scarce lawyers and enabling bounded self-help, rather than replacing comprehensive representation. Their common rationale is a severe capacity gap: AI can move routine drafting, intake, triage and information delivery away from lawyers so professional time is concentrated on judgment, advocacy and higher-stakes matters. They materially develop the proposition through a tiered, risk-sensitive deployment model, bounded tools grounded in official or vetted information, human editing and review, user testing, shared infrastructure, co-development and targeted investment. Internal variation concerns emphasis and ambition rather than the core direction. Slayton and Leonard stress low-risk court information and escalation to human help; Behnke focuses narrowly on lawyer-controlled drafting; Leonard and McCormack support direct self-help but flag sycophancy and mixed experiences; Black combines workflow efficiency with consumer information while questioning commercial incentives; and contributors to the 2025 report go further by advocating shared infrastructure, direct consumer availability and regulatory reform. Most claimed benefits remain prospective, anecdotal or reported capabilities rather than demonstrated effects on legal outcomes, and the sources acknowledge reliability, confidentiality, implementation-capacity and equity risks. Because this is a curated selection, this alignment should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: AI can handle the repetitive and standardized tasks that now consume attorneys’ time, freeing us to focus on the parts of practice that require judgment, empathy, and advocacy.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: So I'm curious about your thoughts on thinking through different ways to select uses that are low-risk—identifying those and rolling out opportunities to test and get feedback from self-represented litigants there—versus the more high-stakes situations where we would want to focus lawyer time and attention (and the promise of AI) to help move lawyers more in that direction.
qs.a: AI in LA Courts: David Slayton on Access to Justice — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The selected AI-native legal-provider sources support the proposition that AI’s principal civil-justice value lies in expanding meaningful legal help rather than merely increasing lawyer productivity. Both connect legal AI to unaffordable or inaccessible services and frame the desired outcome as changed service delivery for clients. Their reasoning is principally prospective, however: neither source demonstrates population-level access gains or supplies detailed evaluation of client outcomes. There is material variation in emphasis. Philip Young focuses on affordable AI-enabled advice for unmet need, especially where vulnerable people face serious legal problems, while treating matter complexity as a boundary on how far technology can substitute for fuller assistance. Ryan Walker more strongly stresses redesigning the service-delivery model and is dissatisfied with selling increasingly capable tools primarily to lawyers and law firms; he also advances a broad automation estimate without providing the underlying methodology. Young therefore aligns more directly with the cluster’s bounded-help framing, whereas Walker reinforces its client-service priority but does not address the proposition’s human-verification, escalation or other safety safeguards. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of all AI-native legal providers.

qs.q: At the moment we have an awful lot of unmet legal need and with AI we can now build tools that at a acceptable cost can provide people with sort of legal advice and legal services that that that they need but can't presently access.
qs.a: Philip Young — Garfield AI: SRA Authorisation, Volume Economics, and the Access-to-Justice Case · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: We'd actually see the service delivery model really change.
qs.a: Ryan Walker — General Legal: Rebuilding the Law Firm, the MSO Structure, and Supervision · AI-native providers · 2026

vlens.an: This curated legal-tech-vendor voice supports the proposition that AI should expand meaningful legal help while preserving human involvement, rather than simply replace comprehensive representation. The strongest common reasons are that AI may reduce time and resource constraints enough for lawyers to accept otherwise impractical matters, and that safe deployment requires humans to remain embedded in workflows for intervention, validation and monitoring. Some sources also reinforce the proposition’s broader service-delivery framing, arguing that investment in tools alone will not close the justice gap without attention to staffing, business models and how more clients are served. Material variation concerns emphasis and evidentiary depth: the Filevine-related source is strongly optimistic about prospective capacity and cost gains but offers little on safeguards; Josef provides a concrete human-in-the-loop model but no quantified proof of safety or capacity gains; the LawNext conversation stresses human verification and service redesign while remaining uncertain about outcomes. The Boehmig, Chiriboga and Rocket Copilot excerpts are broadly compatible with social benefit, augmentation or access to justice, but are too general, introductory or retrospective to establish positions on bounded self-help and safeguards. None of these sources establishes that AI can substitute for comprehensive representation, and several claimed benefits remain predictions or practitioner observations rather than measured findings.

qs.q: And I think what you'll see is there will now be cases that a lawyer would have had to say no to because of the risk or the time burden or the resources that they had available at their firm that they will sort of now open up the aperture for what they could bring and help their clients with.
qs.a: From Customer to Acquirer: Filevine's Ryan Anderson and Pincites' Sona Sulakian on Building AI Contract Intelligence · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: It’s about  building them into the workflow to ensure that the tool is going to operate effectively and safely.
qs.a: RAG is Not Dead: Josef's Sam Flynn on Legal Tech That Works · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition’s core direction and materially develop it through early implementation practices. They frame generative AI primarily as a way to expand legal-aid capacity, improve intake and triage, and provide limited legal information—not as a demonstrated replacement for comprehensive representation. Their clearest contribution is a human-mediated copilot model, supported by community research, frontline-provider consultation, risk assessment and staged demonstration projects. Common reasons include severe unmet civil legal need, the resource burden of triage, and the possibility of redirecting professional time toward higher-value assistance. Material variation remains: Perlman stresses broad hands-on learning rather than deployment design; the access-to-justice panel proposes provider workflows and direct self-help but relies largely on predictions and acknowledges uneven capabilities and privacy concerns; Hagan and Nori offer the most concrete safeguards and implementation pipeline; and Boehmig’s broader call for technologically informed lawyers and socially beneficial development does not address the proposition closely enough to establish his position. Across this curated set, claimed benefits are mainly prospective: the sources describe experiments, use cases and conditional expectations rather than measured improvements in legal outcomes or reductions in unmet need.

qs.q: So that's meant doing a lot of interviews, scenario exercises where we have people try out AI and rate it, talking to providers about what kinds of tasks and opportunities they think should be prioritized, if any, for generative AI R&D, and basically trying to identify an agenda of where AI might be useful or not and how to evaluate quality and risks for these prospective use cases.
qs.a: Margaret Hagan & Sateesh Nori — putting AI to the test for legal services: lab-to-pilot pipelines and the crisis case for urgency · Access to justice · 2024

qs.q: So we built a co-pilot model for these operators so that the Gen AI can be in the background, like a really experienced supervisor, and can feed answers to the person who can then relay them to the caller as a first step.
qs.a: Margaret Hagan & Sateesh Nori — putting AI to the test for legal services: lab-to-pilot pipelines and the crisis case for urgency · Access to justice · 2024

elens.an: Across this curated 2025 set, the sources broadly accept the proposition that AI should expand meaningful civil legal help by redirecting scarce professional time and providing bounded assistance rather than replacing comprehensive representation. They collectively develop that proposition with concrete models: automating intake and routine work while reserving advocacy and difficult questions for professionals; tiering assistance by risk; converting official information into actionable self-help; validating tools with subject-matter experts before launch and monitoring them afterward; and supporting adoption through training, procurement guidance, user research, shared infrastructure and public-interest governance. Material variation concerns ambition, safeguards and evidence. One source envisages direct-to-public systems eventually making legal aid obsolete, which pushes toward substitution beyond the cluster’s bounded framing; others explicitly retain lawyers for high-stakes matters or question whether information alone will help more than a limited share of users. Some focus on improving existing legal-aid capacity, while others argue for redesigning justice around prevention and outcomes. Commercial incentives, unequal implementation capacity and Big Tech governance remain unresolved. Most claimed benefits are prospective, anecdotal or based on reported capabilities; the strongest capacity figures are provider-and-practitioner reports stated as maxima without disclosed evaluation methods. One career-focused source provides too little evidence to assess the proposition. These patterns describe only the supplied curated sources and do not establish prevalence among 2025 commentators or practitioners.

qs.q: It’s about  building them into the workflow to ensure that the tool is going to operate effectively and safely.
qs.a: RAG is Not Dead: Josef's Sam Flynn on Legal Tech That Works · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: I see AI as a tool, not a replacement—it’s a tool.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that AI should expand meaningful legal help by augmenting professional capacity and supporting bounded self-help rather than simply replacing comprehensive representation. They materially develop it through concrete proposals: automate routine intake, drafting, triage and information tasks; redirect lawyers toward judgment, empathy, advocacy and appeals; use tiered service models; build shared, vetted infrastructure; and invest in implementation capacity. Human oversight is explicit in some accounts, including cross-checking AI output and extensive lawyer editing, while complexity is treated as a limit on autonomous assistance. Material variation remains. Some sources principally predict lower costs and greater case capacity without detailing safeguards; Nori explores more autonomous dispute resolution but offers a human-adjudicator fallback; and the Microsoft Legal source redirects the framing toward outcome-led in-house service delivery for business clients rather than unmet civil legal need. The Rocket Copilot introduction is too preliminary to establish a developed position. Across the period, most claimed access and capacity benefits remain practitioner expectations, anecdotes or proposed business models rather than independently measured outcomes, and implementation inequality, reliability and regulation remain unresolved.

qs.q: AI can handle the repetitive and standardized tasks that now consume attorneys’ time, freeing us to focus on the parts of practice that require judgment, empathy, and advocacy.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2026
